title: Compiling Known Rules into Compact Neural Agents: Weight-Space Programming on Unseen Games
domain: games (ARC-AGI-3-style interactive grid games), reinforcement learning

headline_result.text: On 20 private unseen games, the best writer's weights in a fixed 57k actor solved 56% of held-out-level episodes with feedback while the same writers' Python programs solved 97-100%, and a single standard PPO update destroyed most written-weight success.
headline_result.quote: the best writer’s networks solve 56% of episodes on held-out levels with feedback, but the four strongest writers’ Python programs solve 97–100%, and the gap grows with game difficulty.

evidence_quality.n_runs_or_seeds: 3 runs per writer and family (ablations 1 run; PPO 3 seeds)

key_claims.claim: Written networks with a free architecture are programs in network form: almost all parameters are exactly zero and most of the rest are small integers or powers of two, and bounded NumPy programs do better.
key_claims.quote: 93% of their parameters are exactly zero, 90% of the rest are small integers or powers of two, and NumPy programs with the same loop rules and caps solve 91% against the networks’ 79%.

key_claims.claim: Learning the same actor's weights from the support levels transfers far worse than writing them, but this compares information access (source code versus level data).
key_claims.quote: Writers read the source while learners see only those levels, so this compares information access.

key_claims.claim: Written fixed-actor weights are extremely fragile: tiny noise or one PPO update removes most of their success, so writing and RL fine-tuning do not combine.
key_claims.quote: With standard PPO on these binary-success games, writing and RL fine-tuning do not combine.

key_claims.claim: The writers' own architectures, retrained from standard initialisation, solve almost nothing.
key_claims.quote: The best writer’s architectures, trained from standard initialisation within our budget, solve 1%.

key_claims.claim: A one-shot network solved half the held-out episodes only where the same writer's one-shot program also did.
key_claims.quote: Understanding a game well enough to program it thus appears necessary for writing its weights, and expressing that understanding in a fixed network is the hard part.

key_claims.claim: Released language-task networks from another WSP project show the same signature: 99% zeros.
key_claims.quote: we find 99% of the parameters exactly zero and 95% of the rest small integers or powers of two

limitations_stated.text: Binary-success games are a poor testbed for combining writing with RL; RL result rests on 3-4 families.
limitations_stated.quote: Our games have binary success per level, which makes them a poor testbed for combining writing with RL.

limitations_stated.text: Bounded learning budgets; stronger learners might narrow the gap.
limitations_stated.quote: so stronger learners might narrow the gap to written weights.

limitations_stated.text: An evaluated writer designed the harness and analysis; prompts were piloted with evaluated writers.
limitations_stated.quote: An evaluated writer (Claude Opus 5.5) designed the harness and analysis.

notes_for_review: The most rigorous WSP stress test in the corpus: private unseen games, held-out levels and renderings, nine writer models, pre-stated hypotheses, program and learned-weight baselines, closed-loop and perturbation controls, and full request accounting. Its central finding is deflationary: written weights are sparse hand-set programs, worse than the same model's code, not trainable, and destroyed by tiny perturbations. The written-versus-learned comparison is confounded by information access, which the author states. Single author; harness designed with an evaluated model.
